key_terms.meaning: Programs, plus the data they work on, plus the documents that describe and explain them — not code alone.
The facts, numbers and records a program reads and transforms, separate from the instructions themselves.
Specifications, design notes, user manuals and test records that travel with the product and make it maintainable.
Software that solves a business or user problem by processing data for a customer: payroll, billing, a ticket-booking app.
Software burned into a device to control it, with tight limits on memory, power and time.
Products whose main purpose is to run that control software: washing machines, engine controllers, set-top boxes.
Software built around numerical computation and simulation, where wrong arithmetic matters more than pretty screens.
Software that uses pattern learning, search or inference so it can act in situations not written into the code as rules.
Ordinary products that now carry a learning or inference component inside them, so their behaviour can change with training data.
A family of related products built from one shared set of core assets with small variations for each customer.
Engineering style that builds new versions by reusing tested components from earlier products of the same family.
Software rented over a network, run and updated by the provider, paid for by subscription.
Old software still carrying the business even though its structure, language or documentation is poor.
The bottom layer of software engineering: everything above it aims at an agreed level of product quality.
Software development life cycle: the phases a product passes through from initiation to retirement, and their ordering.
The five common activities — communication, planning, modeling, construction, deployment — that every project adapts into its own process.
Work that runs across the whole project rather than in one phase: tracking, risk, quality, configuration management, measurement.
The concrete tasks, deliverables and quality checks chosen to carry out a framework activity on a particular project.
A named, reusable description of a problem-and-solution in process design, applied across many projects.
A sequential lifecycle where each phase is completed before the next begins, with feedback usually only backwards.
A model that delivers the product in successive increments, each one adding working functionality for the user.
An evolutionary model that repeats planning, risk analysis, engineering and evaluation in widening loops.
Development by short repeated increments with working software each cycle, close customer contact, and welcome to changing requirements.
An agile method that adds specific engineering practices such as pair programming, test-first coding and continuous integration.

takeaways: Software is programs plus data plus documents, so a deliverable that is only code is an incomplete product.
The application domain — business, embedded, scientific, AI, product line — decides which engineering practices you need.
Software engineering stands on four layers: quality focus, process, methods and tools; skipping the process layer ruins the other three.
The SDLC gives the phase names; the process model decides how those phases are ordered, repeated and fed back.
Every project adapts the same five framework activities plus umbrella activities into its own task set.
Waterfall suits stable, well-understood requirements; incremental and spiral suit change and risk.
Spiral is the only one of the three classical models that builds a formal risk-analysis step into every loop.
Agile wins on short feedback and customer involvement, but it still needs discipline: XP's practices supply that discipline.
Most project failures trace back to people, process and requirements, and only a minority to pure coding defects.
bank_note: Long answers here are scored on definitions plus comparison: expect questions that ask you to compare two process models or justify a model choice for a given project, so always name the model's phases, its feedback path and its risk handling.

bank.q: Define software. Explain why software is described as programs, data and documents, and list four application domains with one example each.
outline: Definition covering programs, data, documents
Why documents matter: maintenance, handover, testing
Four domains: application, embedded, engineering/scientific, AI or product-line
One concrete example per domain
Note that domain decides practices (e.g. embedded needs timing and memory limits)

bank.q: Explain software engineering as a layered technology. What does each layer contribute, and what happens when a layer is missing?
outline: Four layers: quality focus, process, methods, tools
Quality focus at the base; process as the glue that holds layers
Methods: analysis, design, construction, testing techniques
Tools: CASE, IDE, version control support
Consequence of missing process layer: tools and methods used ad hoc, poor quality and control

bank.q: Describe the generic process framework and explain any five umbrella activities with an example of each.
outline: Five framework activities: communication, planning, modeling, construction, deployment
Definition and purpose of each
Five umbrella activities: tracking and control, risk management, quality assurance, configuration management, measurement
Concrete example per umbrella activity
Point that the framework is adapted, not followed literally

bank.q: Explain the phases of the software development life cycle and state the main deliverable of each phase.
outline: Initiation/feasibility, requirements, design, coding, testing, deployment, maintenance
Deliverables: feasibility report, SRS, design document, source code, test reports, release
Overlap and feedback between phases
Maintenance as the longest and costliest phase
Verification and validation placement

bank.q: List the common software myths held by managers, customers and practitioners, and explain why each is dangerous.
outline: Management myths: more people, more tools, buying hardware fixes it
Customer myths: a general goal is enough, requirements can change freely
Practitioner myths: work is done when code runs, quality is tested in later
Effect: wrong estimates, poor requirements, late discovery of defects
Correct view: process, measurement and early quality work

bank.q: Explain the waterfall model with a diagram, and list its advantages and limitations.
outline: Sequential phases with named deliverables
Feedback generally one phase back
Advantages: simple, documented, milestone-based, good for stable requirements
Limitations: change is costly, working software appears late, risk discovered late
Where it still fits: well-understood, contract-driven, safety-critical projects

bank.q: A retail bank wants a UPI payment feature. Rules from the regulator change every few months and the first release is needed in four months. Choose a process model, and justify it against one alternative.
outline: Identify characteristics: changing external rules, need for early release, high transaction safety
Pick incremental or agile, or an incremental core plus prototype for risky parts
Show how requirements changes are absorbed per increment
Reject pure waterfall because of frozen early requirements
Mention umbrella activities: risk management, configuration management, quality assurance
Add regular releases and regression testing

bank.q: Take one framework activity — say construction — for a hostel mess billing app built by a four-person team, and write its task set.
outline: Name the framework activity and the project context
List concrete tasks in order
Deliverables of each task
Quality checks applied before moving on
Milestone or review point
How the task set differs from a large safety-critical project

bank.q: A small team of five developers agrees to follow Extreme Programming. Describe at least six XP practices they would adopt and how each is carried out day to day.
outline: Planning game and user stories with on-site customer
Small releases, short iterations
Test-first development and automated unit tests
Pair programming and collective code ownership
Continuous integration
Refactoring and simple design
Metaphor/system metaphor optional
Note: XP needs discipline and customer availability

bank.q: An insurance company must move a 15-year-old claim-processing system to a new platform. Explain how you would treat this legacy software, and how reuse could reduce the effort.
outline: Definition of legacy software and its business value
Why not simply discard: embedded business rules, undocumented behaviour
Steps: inventory, reverse engineering, restructuring, reengineering, retirement decision
Reuse: reuse of business rules, data and tested modules; product-line thinking
Risk of skipping documentation and regression testing
Cost-benefit note

bank.q: Analyse why software projects fail. Group the causes under people, process and requirements, and suggest one preventive step for each group.
outline: People: skill gaps, high turnover, unclear roles, poor communication, unrealistic schedules
Process: no defined process, no tracking or measurement, skipped reviews, weak configuration management
Requirements: vague scope, unmanaged change, missing stakeholders
Technical causes as a smaller category, not the whole story
One preventive step per group: training and roles, process with milestones and reviews, requirements baseline with change control
Order-of-magnitude statement that most failures are management and requirement failures

bank.q: Compare the incremental and spiral models. For a large, high-risk defence project, which would you recommend, and why?
outline: Both are evolutionary or repeated-delivery in nature
Incremental: each increment adds usable functionality; no explicit risk step
Spiral: four quadrants per loop — objectives, risk analysis, engineering, customer evaluation
Spiral risk analysis suits high-risk projects; also supports prototypes and staged commitment
Incremental simpler to manage and delivers usable features sooner
Recommendation for defence project: spiral, with justification on risk exposure and evaluation gates
Note spiral's overhead and need for risk expertise

bank.q: A team adopts agile practices but the project still fails. Evaluate the likely reasons and state what agile does and does not guarantee.
outline: Agile assumes customer availability, discipline and small co-located teams
Failure causes: no product owner decisions, no automated tests, no definition of done, poor estimation
Umbrella activities still needed: tracking, configuration management, quality assurance
Agile does not remove the need for requirement clarity, architecture for large systems, or documentation where required
Large or regulated systems need scaling and contracts that allow change
Conclusion: practices help, but people and process causes remain decisive

bank.q: Assess the suitability of the waterfall model for a safety-critical embedded product such as a railway signalling controller, and contrast it with an agile approach.
outline: Embedded domain traits: timing, memory limits, hardware dependence, certification needs
Waterfall strengths here: documented phases, traceability, formal reviews and verification at each stage
Weakness: late feedback on real hardware, change expensive
Agile strengths: early feedback, continuous testing; weaknesses: certification evidence and hardware dependency
Hybrid suggestion: planned phases with iterative prototyping and continuous integration in later stages
Criteria: cost of change, need for traceability, external safety standards

glossary.def: The application of a systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to the development, operation and maintenance of software.
The set of activities, their ordering, and the constraints and resources that produce a software product.
A simplified, organised description of how a project will move through the lifecycle phases.
One of the five broad work areas of the generic process framework: communication, planning, modeling, construction, deployment.
Project-wide work such as tracking, risk management, quality assurance, configuration management and measurement that applies in every phase.
Examination of an organisation's process against a reference model to find improvement priorities.
Comparing actual progress and cost against the plan and taking corrective action.
Identifying, analysing, planning for and monitoring events that could harm the project.
Identifying, controlling and recording changes to work products so versions and variants stay under control.
Planned activities and checks that give confidence the process and product meet agreed standards.
Eliciting, analysing, specifying and validating what the software must do.
Software requirements specification: the agreed written statement of required behaviour and constraints.
An early check of whether the proposed system is technically, economically and operationally workable.
Checking that the product was built correctly according to its specification.
Checking that the right product was built — that it meets the user's real need.
A partial or rough working version built to learn about requirements or technical risk before full development.
One pass through the development activities that produces a tested, runnable result.
The piece of usable functionality added to the product by one iteration.
The ordered list of work items or features still to be built, reordered as priorities change.
Improving the internal structure of working code without changing what it does.
Two developers working at one machine, one writing code and the other reviewing as it is written.
Merging each developer's work into the shared build many times a day, with automated tests run on every merge.
Any person or group affected by the system or able to influence its requirements.
A short authorising document that states the project's purpose, scope, objectives and key people.
